stanzas: Puhuruhuru nana nei i tiki mai
orig.credit: Te Rauparaha, Ngāti Toa Rangatira (c. 1820); the text as set out in the Haka Ka Mate Attribution Act 2014 (New Zealand)

stanzas: It is death! It is death!
It is life! It is life!
It is death! It is death!
It is life! It is life!
The hairy one, who himself fetched
One step up, another step up
One step up, another step up

notes: line 1.1-4: 'Ka mate' / 'Ka ora' can be read as 'I die' / 'I live' or 'it is death' / 'it is life'; Te Rauparaha is said to have chanted it while hiding from his pursuers, unsure whether he would be found.

line 1.6: the source splits the phrase 'tangata puhuruhuru / nana nei i tiki mai / whakawhiti te ra' differently from the usual lineation; translated line by line as given. 'Puhuruhuru' is hairy; who the hairy man is (traditionally the chief Te Wharerangi, who sheltered him, though this is debated) is disputed, so it stays literal.
line 1.7: 'Whakawhiti te ra' is 'caused the sun to shine (or to cross over)'; the clause is 'who fetched (the sun) and made it shine'.
line 1.8-9: 'Upane' is a step, a terrace or a rank (of warriors); 'step by step, upward' is the usual sense, but the word is disputed.
Macrons: the Act's text as imported has none (Tenei for Tēnei, Puhuruhuru for Pūhuruhuru, Nana for Nāna, ra for rā); left as it stands.
